title: Field investigations: population size and distribution
aim: To use random sampling with quadrats to estimate the population size of a common plant species (daisies) in two areas, and to use a transect to investigate how its distribution changes with an abiotic factor (light intensity).
background: It is usually impossible to count every organism in a habitat, so ecologists take samples. A quadrat is a square frame, often 50 cm × 50 cm (an area of 0.25 m²), placed on the ground so the number of a plant species inside it can be counted. Quadrats must be placed randomly so the sample is representative and not biased by the person choosing where to look.

The mean number of organisms per quadrat can be used to estimate the population size of a species in the whole area: estimated population = mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ area of one quadrat). Comparing the mean number per quadrat in two areas shows whether a species is more abundant in one area than the other. For plants that are hard to count individually, such as grass, percentage cover can be estimated instead.

A transect is a line, such as a tape measure, laid across a habitat where conditions change, for example from shade under a tree into an open field. Quadrats are placed at regular intervals along it, and the number of organisms is recorded in each, along with abiotic factors such as light intensity, soil moisture or temperature. This shows how the distribution of a species changes along the gradient.
hypothesis: Daisies will be more abundant in the open field than in the shaded area under trees, and along a transect from the tree into the open field the number of daisies per quadrat will increase as light intensity increases.

variables.independent: Area sampled (open field or shaded area under trees) for random sampling; distance from the tree (and therefore light intensity) for the transect.
control: Same size of quadrat (0.25 m²) throughout
Same number of quadrats sampled in each area (10)
Same method of deciding which plants to count (count a plant if more than half of it is inside the quadrat)
Sampling done on the same day, so weather and season are the same
Same species identified using the same identification key

equipment: Two long tape measures (for example 30 m)
Random number generator (calculator, app or random number table)
Identification key or photographs of the species
Tent pegs or markers to hold the tape measures
method: Random sampling: in the open field, lay out two tape measures at right angles along two edges of the area to be sampled (for example 30 m × 20 m) to form a grid.
Use a random number generator to produce two numbers, to use as coordinates (for example 12 m along the first tape and 7 m along the second).
Place the bottom left corner of the quadrat at these coordinates.
Count the number of daisy plants inside the quadrat. Count a plant if more than half of it is inside the frame, and record the number.
Repeat with new random coordinates until you have sampled 10 quadrats.
Repeat steps 1 to 5 in the shaded area under the trees.
Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat in each area, and use the total area of each to estimate the population size.
Transect: lay a tape measure in a straight line from the base of a tree out into the open field (for example 20 m long).
Place a quadrat at the start of the tape (0 m) and count the daisies in it.
Measure the light intensity at ground level in the quadrat using a light meter.
Move the quadrat along the tape at regular intervals (every 4 m) and repeat the count and light reading at each point.
Repeat the transect in at least two other places nearby and calculate the mean number of daisies at each distance. Plot the number of daisies and light intensity against distance from the tree.

safety.hazard: Uneven ground, holes and tape measures across the ground
safety.precaution: Walk, do not run, look where you are going and keep tape measures flat and visible.

safety.hazard: Plants, animal faeces and stinging insects
safety.risk: Stings, allergic reactions or infections from contaminated soil.
safety.precaution: Wear gloves if handling plants or soil, tell the teacher about allergies (such as to bee or wasp stings), cover cuts and wash hands afterwards.

safety.risk: Sunburn, getting cold or wet, or getting lost or separated from the group.
safety.precaution: Wear suitable clothing and sun cream, stay within the agreed area and work in groups with a teacher present.

headers: Number of daisies: shaded area under trees
results.notes: Quadrat area = 0.5 m × 0.5 m = 0.25 m². Open field area = 600 m², so the number of quadrats that would fit = 600 ÷ 0.25 = 2400, and the estimated population = 3.0 × 2400 = 7200 daisies. Shaded area = 200 m², so 200 ÷ 0.25 = 800 quadrats and estimated population = 0.5 × 800 = 400 daisies. Mean density in the open field = 3.0 ÷ 0.25 = 12 daisies per m². Transect results (mean of three transects), distance from tree (m): number of daisies (light intensity in lux): 0 m: 0 (2000); 4 m: 1 (5000); 8 m: 3 (11 000); 12 m: 6 (18 000); 16 m: 8 (22 000); 20 m: 9 (23 000). Plot a bar chart to compare the two areas, and a line graph (or kite diagram) for the transect.

analysis: The mean number of daisies per quadrat was 3.0 in the open field and 0.5 in the shaded area. Daisies were six times more abundant per quadrat in the open field.

The estimated population of daisies is 7200 in the 600 m² open field and 400 in the 200 m² shaded area. These are estimates: the true values could be different because only 10 quadrats (2.5 m²) were sampled in each area.

Along the transect, the number of daisies increased from 0 at the base of the tree to 9 at 20 m, as light intensity increased from 2000 lux to 23 000 lux. There is a positive correlation between light intensity and the number of daisies.

A likely explanation is that daisies are small plants that need plenty of light for photosynthesis. Under the trees, the canopy absorbs much of the light, so daisies cannot photosynthesise enough to grow well. However, correlation does not prove cause: other factors that change near trees, such as soil moisture, competition for water and minerals with tree roots, and leaf litter, could also be involved.
The counts in the open field varied from 0 to 6 per quadrat, which shows that daisies are not evenly distributed. Taking more quadrats would give a more representative mean.

errors.error: Too few quadrats were sampled, so the mean may not represent the whole area.
errors.improvement: Sample more quadrats (for example 20 or 30) in each area, until the running mean stops changing much.

errors.error: Deciding whether a plant at the edge of the quadrat is inside or outside is inconsistent.
errors.improvement: Agree a rule before starting, such as counting a plant only if more than half of it is inside the quadrat.

errors.error: Light intensity changes during the day as clouds pass, so readings along the transect are not directly comparable.
errors.improvement: Take light readings at all points as quickly as possible, take several readings at each point and use the mean, or sample on a day with even cloud cover.

errors.error: Plants may be misidentified, or small plants may be missed.
errors.improvement: Use an identification key or photographs, and search each quadrat carefully, perhaps with a gridded quadrat divided into 100 small squares.

examTips: Use random sampling (random coordinates on a grid) to compare two areas, and a transect when conditions change across a habitat.
Learn the population estimate: mean number per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area). Check that both areas are in the same units (m²).
A 50 cm × 50 cm quadrat has an area of 0.25 m², not 2500 m² or 0.5 m²: convert cm to m before multiplying.
Explain why random placement matters: it avoids bias, so the sample is representative.
A correlation between an abiotic factor and the number of organisms does not prove that factor is the cause: other factors may also change.

questions.question: Why should quadrats be placed randomly when comparing the number of daisies in two fields?
options: To avoid bias, so the samples are representative of each field
To make sure every quadrat contains some daisies
So that fewer quadrats are needed
markScheme: 1 mark: to avoid bias / so the sample is representative
questions.explanation: If the student chooses where to put the quadrat, they may tend to pick areas with more (or fewer) daisies. Random placement removes this bias. Random sampling may include quadrats with no daisies, which is a genuine result.

questions.question:
A student counted the number of daisies in 10 quadrats: 3, 0, 5, 2, 4, 1, 6, 3, 2, 4.
Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat.
questions.explanation: Add all the counts (30) and divide by the number of quadrats (10). Remember to include the quadrat with 0 daisies in the count of quadrats.

questions.question:
A field has an area of 600 m². The mean number of daisies in a 0.25 m² quadrat was 3.0.
Estimate the number of daisies in the field.
markScheme: 1 mark: number of quadrats in field = 600 ÷ 0.25 = 2400
questions.explanation: Work out how many quadrats would fit into the field (2400), then multiply by the mean per quadrat. Multiplying 3.0 by 600 (giving 1800) ignores the fact that each quadrat is only 0.25 m².

questions.question:
A square quadrat has sides of 50 cm.
Calculate its area in m².
questions.explanation: Convert to metres first: 50 cm = 0.5 m. Then 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m². A common mistake is to calculate 50 × 50 = 2500 and then divide by 100, giving 25 m²; there are 10 000 cm² in 1 m².

questions.question: A student wants to find out how the distribution of plants changes from the edge of a pond to dry ground. Which sampling method is most suitable?
options: Placing quadrats at regular intervals along a transect
Placing quadrats randomly across the whole area
Counting every plant in the area
Placing one quadrat where the most plants grow
markScheme: 1 mark: a transect with quadrats at regular intervals
questions.explanation: A transect is used when conditions change gradually across a habitat. Random sampling is best for comparing two separate areas, and counting every plant is usually impossible.

questions.question: Describe how a student could place quadrats randomly in a field.
markScheme: 1 mark: lay two tape measures at right angles to make a grid (axes)
1 mark: use a random number generator to give coordinates and place the quadrat there
questions.explanation: Using random coordinates means every point in the field has an equal chance of being sampled. Throwing the quadrat over your shoulder is not truly random and could be dangerous.

questions.question: Name one abiotic factor that could be measured along a transect, and the piece of equipment used to measure it.
acceptedAnswers: soil pH pH meter or indicator
markScheme: 1 mark: abiotic factor, for example light intensity, temperature, soil moisture, soil pH
1 mark: matching equipment: light meter, thermometer, moisture meter, pH meter or universal indicator
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living features of the environment. Measuring them along a transect allows you to look for a correlation with the distribution of organisms.

questions.question:
The mean number of daisies in a 0.25 m² quadrat was 3.0.
Calculate the mean number of daisies per m².
markScheme: 1 mark: 1 m² is 4 quadrats (1 ÷ 0.25 = 4)
1 mark: 3.0 × 4 = 12 daisies per m²
questions.explanation: Each quadrat covers a quarter of a square metre, so multiply by 4 (or divide 3.0 by 0.25) to get 12 per m². Dividing by 4 instead would give 0.75, which is too small.

questions.question:
The numbers of buttercups in seven quadrats were: 2, 5, 3, 8, 4, 6, 1.
What is the median number of buttercups per quadrat?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4 (ordered values: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8)
questions.explanation: Put the values in order (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8) and take the middle one, which is 4. Taking the middle value without ordering first gives 8, which is wrong.

questions.question: A student sampled only three quadrats in a large field. Explain why the estimate of population size may not be accurate.
markScheme: 1 mark: the plants are not evenly distributed (counts vary between quadrats)
1 mark: so a small sample may not be representative of the whole field; more quadrats are needed
questions.explanation: With so few samples, one unusual quadrat could have a big effect on the mean. The more quadrats sampled, the closer the mean is likely to be to the true value.

questions.question: What is a population?
options: All the organisms of different species living in a habitat
The place where an organism lives
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat
A community and its non-living environment
markScheme: 1 mark: all the organisms of one species living in a habitat
questions.explanation: A population is one species. All the populations of different species living together form a community. A community together with its abiotic environment is an ecosystem.

questions.question: Grass is difficult to count as individual plants. Suggest how a student could record the abundance of grass in a quadrat.
acceptedAnswers: count squares in a gridded quadrat
markScheme: 1 mark: estimate the percentage cover (the percentage of the quadrat area covered by grass)
1 mark: for example, use a quadrat divided into 100 small squares and count the squares more than half covered by grass
questions.explanation: Percentage cover is used for plants that grow in mats or clumps. A gridded quadrat makes the estimate more objective and repeatable.

questions.question:
Along a transect from a tree into an open field, the number of daisies increased as light intensity increased.
Suggest an explanation for this, and explain why the student cannot be sure light is the only cause.
markScheme: 1 mark: more light means more photosynthesis, so more glucose for growth (daisies grow better)
1 mark: other factors also change with distance from the tree, such as soil moisture, competition with tree roots for water and minerals, or leaf litter
1 mark: so the correlation does not prove that light is the cause
questions.explanation: A good answer gives a biological explanation and then recognises that a correlation in a field study cannot rule out other variables, because they cannot be controlled.

questions.question: Describe how a student could use quadrats to compare the population of daisies in a sunny field and a shaded field.
markScheme: Indicative content: lay out two tape measures at right angles to make a grid in the first field; use a random number generator to produce coordinates; place quadrat at coordinates; count daisies in quadrat (rule for those on the edge); repeat for at least 10 quadrats; repeat the same in the second field with the same size quadrat and same number of quadrats; calculate mean number per quadrat for each field; measure area of each field; estimate population = mean per quadrat × total area ÷ quadrat area; compare means or estimated populations; sample on the same day
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method describing random placement, counting, repeats, calculation of a mean, and how to compare the two fields or estimate population size.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most key steps, but missing detail of how randomness is achieved or how the data are processed.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as putting quadrats down and counting daisies, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key features are a genuinely random method, enough repeats, the same quadrat size and number in each field, and a clear way of comparing results, such as means or population estimates.

questions.question: Describe how a student could use a transect to investigate how the distribution of daisies changes with light intensity from the base of a tree out into an open field.
markScheme: Indicative content: lay a tape measure in a straight line from the base of the tree into the open field; place a quadrat at regular intervals along the tape (for example every 2 m or 4 m); count the daisies in each quadrat; measure light intensity with a light meter at each quadrat at ground level; take light readings at the same time or quickly to reduce effect of changing cloud; repeat the transect in other places and calculate means; plot number of daisies and light intensity against distance; look for a correlation

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear method describing the transect line, quadrats at regular intervals, counting daisies, measuring light intensity with a light meter, and repeating or presenting the data.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as putting quadrats along a line and counting daisies, without measuring light or giving intervals.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Unlike random sampling, a transect places quadrats systematically at regular intervals so that changes across the habitat can be linked to an abiotic factor measured at the same points.
